BlaÅ¾ys / LRT RÅ«ta Å½ilinskÄ from Alytus dreamed of building a life in the United States. However, after spending several years across the Atlantic, she was forced to turn back. When she and her husband moved to the US, they chose Seattle. RÅ«ta admits they were shocked by the prices at first. Everything in America seemed three times more expensive, and it took them some time to find somewhere to live. â Still, RÅ«ta kept reminding herself that the US had been her dream, and she bravely embraced the challenges. â "At that moment, I wasn't afraid at all because I had dreamed about it for so many years. The streets were full of people, and I would go outside thinking: 'I'm in America, I did it,'" RÅ«ta recalls. â After the coronavirus pandemic, rents in Seattle almost doubled. RÅ«ta and Tomas received a call telling them they had a month to decide whether to renew their lease â instead of $2,700, they would have to pay $4,000. â At the time, RÅ«ta was not working because she was looking after their son. She and her husband realised they could not afford the higher rent on his salary. In a desperate situation, they asked one of his colleagues for advice. He told them about Austin, Texas, its friendly people and warm weather. RÅ«ta Å½ilinskÄ | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT "We looked at each other â we didn't really have much choice. I'd never been there, but we trusted him. My husband needed to find a new position at Amazon so that we could be transferred," RÅ«ta recalls. â Facing anti-immigrant sentiment â The family settled in a suburb of Austin. As RÅ«ta puts it, there was little there apart from identical houses, fields and a few large shops. And although people initially seemed friendly, that later changed. â "I couldn't stand watching how immigrants were treated â Mexicans and everyone who does the hardest jobs. Those real Americans there simply hate us," RÅ«ta says. â After her son was a little older, RÅ«ta went into real estate. Although she enjoyed the work, she says that as a foreigner she had to work many times harder to prove her worth. Later, other difficulties began. â "I cried for days. We couldn't go to doctors even though we had insurance because you still have to pay thousands when you go there. We brought two puppies with us. One of them became ill, and we took him to the vet. â "They said the operation would cost $15,000, and there was no guarantee he would survive. I spent about $6,000 on treatment, but eventually I lost the dog. After that, everything started going downhill. Every morning I would wake up and think about how we were going to get through that day," she says. RÅ«ta Å½ilinskÄ | Personal archives â Becoming a marshall Eventually, RÅ«ta's husband lost his job during a wave of redundancies. The family decided to move into Austin itself. RÅ«ta's husband found a job at Apple; they found a nice flat and a good school for their son. Meanwhile, RÅ«ta, who had loved cars and racing since childhood, got her first job as a track marshal at a MotoGP race. â As she puts it, that was when she began to hope that life was getting back on track. â "I was very scared because I had never entered that racing world before. I thought it was a man's world. I couldn't sleep the night before, but when I walked into that tent, my whole life changed. Those people welcomed me very warmly because we all volunteer. âThere isn't a single person who is forced to be there because nobody gets paid. Everyone is there because they really want to be, and there is no competition. I came home the happiest person in the world," RÅ«ta says. â Throughout the weekend, she tried to make as many contacts as possible and learn as much as she could because she dreamed of working at Formula One races. According to RÅ«ta, getting there is normally difficult, and people often need to work at least 10 to 15 other races first. â But she was lucky â through recommendations from others, she was offered the chance to work at the Formula One race in Miami. â "It's hard work. Fifteen hours a day. Sun, heat or rain â it doesn't matter. There would be no racing without marshals, whether it's Formula One or a rally in Lithuania. Every race has marshals because they prepare the track. We check whether everything is OK and whether everything is ready. There are two types of marshal. â "If something happens and you see flags, those are track marshals. The second type are those who run onto the track when there is an accident. That's me, because I need the action. I won't lie â when I first had to run out and help lift a motorcyclist, the adrenaline kicked in," she says. Xenophobic attacks However, the longer she stayed in America, the more unsafe she felt, and she could not come to terms with the hostility towards immigrants. â RÅ«ta says her family also found themselves in several dangerous situations. â "It got to the point where my husband was heard speaking at a petrol station by several Americans. They realised from his accent that he was an immigrant, then followed him to our home, pulled him out of the car and started beating him. Because we lived in an apartment complex, a lot of guys came running and helped him. â "I've had someone threaten me with a gun outside a shop, even though I was with my child. I couldn't take my eyes off my son. I started thinking about what his life would be like here," RÅ«ta recalls. â The final straw was an incident involving her dream car. Watching from her balcony as a tow truck drove away with a car, she initially thought someone else had had some bad luck â until she realised it was her car. â RÅ«ta says the car had been towed because of an administrative error: a bank employee had failed to record in the paperwork that the family had already paid it off. â "It took so much fighting to get the car back. But then I told my husband I couldn't do it any more. We started talking about what to do. Our original plan was to leave after a year, once we'd saved some money. Eventually, we both decided to start looking for jobs in Lithuania. â "Our rule was that once either of us found a job, we would leave. My husband got a job, so there was no reason to wait. We had two months to sort everything out. I sold everything at home, leaving just two mattresses and a sofa so we'd have somewhere to sleep," RÅ«ta says of their decision to leave America. â She says there was another reason she wanted to return â her parents. She also wanted her son to grow up seeing his grandparents and other relatives. â "My mother is 70, and my father is 75. I calculated that if I stayed in America, I wouldn't see my parents very often. It sent a shiver down my spine to think that I might be able to count the number of times we would see each other on my fingers," RÅ«ta says. RÅ«ta Å½ilinskÄ | Personal archives A difficult start back home â RÅ«ta returned to Vilnius last December, acknowledging that she knew returning home would be extremely difficult. And the years she spent abroad had distanced her even further. â "I left here when I was 18. I was a child. My entire adult life was in England and America. So I'm already different; I think differently. It was definitely a shock. â "For some reason, I was very afraid of coming back. Perhaps it was also my ego â I had left, I had to be there and prove something to myself, so coming back felt like giving up, like a disappointment. I had to start everything again," she says. â After returning, she had to get used to everything â an unfamiliar city, the way people interacted and bureaucracy. And although she cried a lot during the first five months, RÅ«ta now looks at everything with hope. â She says she quickly noticed how much Lithuania had changed. Previously, when she returned only for holidays to visit relatives, RÅ«ta did not have time to explore the countryside or the city at her leisure. â Compared with the US, she sees a number of advantages in Lithuania. Previously used to dealing with everything together with her husband, they now both know they are not alone â their family is here. â Their son also feels very comfortable in Lithuania. RÅ«ta is happy that she feels safe here, both for herself and for him. â "I'm not afraid even at night in Lithuania. Although some people say you need to be careful, I say I've survived in America, so I'm not afraid here," RÅ«ta says. â Her interest in cars and motorsport did not disappear after returning home. RÅ«ta is actively exploring opportunities to work in the field in Lithuania, attends racing events and has already worked as a marshal at the Formula One round in Belgium. â "Everything is possible from Lithuania too," RÅ«ta says. https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/germany-inve.text: RSS Diary Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 Europe Germany investigates ‘state-sponsored sabotage’ after attacks on power grids Police say they are investigating whether a sabotage attempt near Cologne was linked to an earlier attack on a substation close to a major power plant in Brandenburg Ayhan Simsek 02 September 2026 • Update : 02 September 2026 BERLIN Germany is investigating “state-sponsored sabotage and left-wing extremism” after an attempted attack on the power grid near Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said Wednesday. Reul told a news conference that there was an “initial suspicion” of an anti-constitutional act after unidentified suspects targeted a substation in the Rheidt district of Bergheim. Officials are examining two possibilities, “foreign-state directed sabotage and left-wing extremism,” he said, adding that neither can be ruled out. “That was intentional, that was a crime,” Reul said. “Whoever goes after that is attacking our country.” He said the suspects apparently placed conductive material — possibly cables — on an overhead line, causing a short circuit. Police were called to the site Tuesday evening after witnesses reported bright flashes, local media reported. Several lines were affected. Officers sealed off a wide area, deployed a helicopter and expanded the crime-scene search. Investigators weigh link between attacks Michael Esser, criminal director of the Cologne police, told reporters they had found six devices in the area believed to be connected to the sabotage attempt. The devices were designed to use pyrotechnic items to propel a wire upward and over power lines, causing short circuits on extra-high-voltage lines. “Our investigation is still in its early stages. We are classifying this act as an attack on critical infrastructure,” Esser said. “Naturally, we are also examining potential links to a recent incident in Brandenburg. We are working very closely with our colleagues there,” he added, but declined to provide further details. Earlier on Tuesday, unidentified suspects carried out a similar sabotage attack on an electrical facility near the Jaenschwalde plant, one of Germany’s largest brown-coal power stations in eastern Brandenburg near the Polish border. Using a similar homemade device and pyrotechnic items, they caused short circuits on extra-high-voltage lines. Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said authorities were investigating in all directions. “We cannot currently rule out any particular perpetrators,” he said. “This is a hybrid threat we are currently witnessing, and as such, we cannot rule out the possibility that foreign powers are behind it.” Brandenburg police said they are also investigating whether a terrorist organization could be behind the sabotage attempt. A spokesman for the Federal Interior Ministry told Anadolu that authorities were investigating whether the recent sabotage attempts were linked and whether they formed part of hybrid attacks by foreign powers. “They are all the subject of ongoing investigations,” the spokesman said, adding that the results would be shared with the media once officials had solid findings. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All Turkish Grand Prix announces return dates to Formula 1 racing action IMO urges member states to stop attacking merchant ships Global markets trade mixed ahead of Fed’s rate decision Yemeni army targets Houthi positions in western Taiz Kosovo's ex-President Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes EU to introduce common age limit for social media EU Commission chief calls for new European Security Council,' bloc-wide emergency security protocol See All Homemade rockets used in attempted attack on Brandenburg power plant: Report Turkish defense minister discusses defense, security issues with British counterpart

https://www.dw.com/en/finland-the-world-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nl7M Finland's policymakers will spend the winter deciding where the ax should fall Image: Ardan Fuessmann/IMAGO Advertisement There's an uneasy mood in Finland , the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years. With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts. Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression. Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%. Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers. The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026. EU scrutiny over growing deficit Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn. "The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW. Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031. Finland: Europe's race for critical raw materials To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video National Coalition rules out tax hikes To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts. While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt. Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts." While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%. With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy. "More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW. Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion. Finland has hiked up defense spending, and recently received its first delivery of F-35 fighter jets Image: Jeremy Lock/REUTERS Finland rearms after Russia's full-scale invasion Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion. During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target. A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war , the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war. While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year. On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth. "There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong. Despite the country's financial woes, Finns are consistently ranked as the world’s happiest people Image: Depositphotos/IMAGO Markets give Helsinki time to reform Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating. On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe. That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France. Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.
